title: Lexical prefetch and hybrid batching — runtime boundary sketch
content:
Purpose:
This is a working sketch for shifting some tokenization work across the runtime boundary to reduce median tail latency while preserving batching efficiency and correctness. Avoids re-using earlier "tokenizer" doc wordings; focuses on a lexical-stage model, hybrid prefetch, and a compact prefix kvstore integration.

Context / motivation:
- Observed pain: small requests (user messages < 64 chars) dominate P50 latency even when model generation is fast because tokenization and per-request RPC overheads are not amortized.
- Large requests benefit from existing batched tokenization pools, but small, latency-sensitive traffic needs a different flow.
- We want a single API surface for callers but an internal hybrid pipeline that routes requests to eager or lazy lexicalization paths based on request characteristics and SLOs.

High-level design idea:
1) Lexical stage (lightweight, deterministic): run cheap normalization + subword boundary detection in a very low-latency compiled path (C++/WASM). Output: normalized string segments and a small fingerprint for prefix-cache lookup. This should be embeddable in edge points (LB or local agent) eventually.
2) Hybrid batching router: a small dispatcher that decides per-request path:
   - Fast-path (micro): if normalized length < N and SLO tight -> do local lexicalization and a microbatch request to model with on-demand embedding of token ids (no heavy tokenization).
   - Batch-path (bulk): for longer inputs or throughput-optimized requests -> route to the tokenization worker pool that performs full tokenization and emits token ids for runtime.
3) Compact prefix store (lexeme-kvstore): a shared in-memory prefix cache keyed by (model, vocab-hash, normalized-prefix-hash). Stores KV entries of the form {prefix-length, token-ids, partial-kv-state-hash}. Used by runtime to avoid recomputing tokenization for common prefixes.
4) Runtime integration: runtime accepts either: (a) token_id stream + full kv-cache state (existing flow), or (b) a prefix-hash reference and lexical checksum so runtime looks up/merges cached tokenization state and resumes decoding.

Boundary contract (minimal API sketch):
- Client -> Tokenizer: POST /lexicalize { model_id, model_version, text, want_prefix_handle: bool, priority_hint } returns { norm_text, prefix_handle?(string), small_token_preview(list of ints, optional), lexical_latency_ms }
- Tokenizer -> Runtime: POST /start_decode { model_id, version, prefix_handle | token_ids, decode_cfg }
Rules: prefix_handle is a stable opaque key valid for N seconds and includes the normalization and vocab-hash in its scope. If token_ids provided, runtime treats as authoritative. If prefix_handle provided, runtime attempts local lexeme-kvstore lookup and falls back to full tokenize RPC if a miss.

Cache key schema proposal (compact):
- key = sha1(model_id || "|" || vocab_hash || "|" || normalizer_version || "|" || first_64_bytes_of_norm_text)
- value = serialized { token_ids_prefix (delta-compressed), tokenizer-version, normalized-length, last-touch-ts }
- Hot-set protection: maintain a small MRU ring of frequently accessed keys pinned for a longer TTL to reduce evictions during bursts.

Eviction policy and coherence:
- LRU with frequency boost for keys that hit > X times in sliding window.
- Invalidate on model version or vocab update; tokenizer service must bump normalizer_version to avoid stale hits.
- Use a versioned prefix handle containing the normalizer_version and vocab_hash so runtime refuses mismatched entries.

Batching semantics and scheduling:
- Microbatches (fast-path) group requests for the model with small per-request token lists. Microbatch window configurable (e.g., 4–8ms) and limited to small total token budget (<=128 tokens) to avoid head-of-line blocking.
- Bulk batches use the existing batching logic but accept prefix handles instead of raw token ids; the tokenizer worker expands handles to token ids during batch creation. Batch planner can choose to expand handles in parallel to model scheduling to hide tokenization latency.
- Backpressure: if tokenizer workers saturate, router will automatically demote fast-path requests to bulk-path after a short retry window to preserve throughput. Exponential backoff with jitter.

KVstore and prefix merging semantics:
- When runtime fetches a prefix handle, it may receive partial kv-state (KV checksum + list of tokens). The runtime must merge token ids into the model's KV cache deterministically. We must define a merge op: append-only for standard left-to-right decoding; for streaming edits we provide a replace flow.
- For safety, runtime rejects prefix handles whose tokenization length does not match the expected normalized-length header. This prevents subtle shift bugs.

Metrics and observability (instrumentation to add):
- lexicalize_latency_p50/p90/p99 (ms)
- prefix_handle_hit_rate (%)
- tokenizer_worker_utilization (%)
- microbatch_wait_ms (avg)
- model_batch_fill_ratio (tokens/slot)
- decode_failure_rate_when_using_prefix_handle (%)
- prefix_eviction_rate, prefix_pin_rate
- end-to-end P50/P90 for short requests and long requests separately (to measure regressions)

Experiment plan (quick A/B):
A: baseline (current full-tokenize-in-worker flow)
B: lex-stage + microbatch router with prefix-handle caching
Metrics: P50/P90 for short requests, model throughput, prefix_hit_rate. Run per-model and aggregate by request size buckets (<32 chars, 32-128, >128). Traffic split 5%/95% initial ramp, monitor 24h before increasing.

Tradeoffs / risks:
- Complexity: extra code-paths increase maintenance cost and test surface. Need robust integration tests for prefix mismatch cases.
- Consistency: must ensure token ids are stable across tokenizer versions and normalizers; otherwise prefix cache causes corruption.
- Security: prefix handles are opaque but could leak text-derived fingerprints. Sign/rotate handles and limit TTL.
- Memory: prefix store needs capacity planning; evictions under load could cause cascading slowdowns. Consider persistent LRU tiers (RAM + local SSD) for larger clusters.

Open questions / TODOs:
- What is a safe N (normalized length) threshold for fast-path? Start with 64 chars, iterate with experiments.
- Should we make the lexical stage language-aware (language id first) to improve normalization? Opt-in for now.
- Exact prefix-handle encoding: opaque vs signed JWT-style vs server-only opaque id. Signed handle gives client-side routing at LB but introduces rotation complexity.
- Where to run lexical stage for hosted vs private deployments? Provide both: local agent for private and shared tokenizer pool for hosted.

Next steps and actionable items:
- Spike: implement a minimal lexicalizer in C++ with normalization + small hashed output (2 engineer-weeks). Assign: Jordan Kim.
- Build a prefix-handle shim in tokenizer service and in runtime codepath to consume it (3 engineer-weeks). Assign: Miguel/ Priya.
- Add metrics and a canary experiment harness; create a dashboard (SLOs + prefix hit rate).
- Document contract in a formal API spec doc and create integration tests (unit tests + cross-process e2e).

Notes to self / rough thoughts:
- Keep tokenization deterministic across platforms (WASM vs native) by tying to a canonical normalizer library.
- Consider using compact varint encoding for token-id prefixes in cache to save memory.
- If prefix hits exceed 70% for short-requests traffic, we can reduce microbatch window aggressively to favor latency.

References and links:
- Related tickets: ENG-1284 (router changes), ENG-1393 (prefix cache design), PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/742
- Slack thread: #serving-runtime tokenization experiments (thread id 3942)

This is a sketch. Feedback welcome — especially on the cache key design and prefix-handle lifetime.

-- Asha
